entry.title: Assign a fresh media asset id when content actually changes
entry.content:
Assign a fresh media asset id when content actually changes

processMediaFile always reused a filename's existing asset id, even when
the new content genuinely differed from what was there before (exactly
what happened when the zstd-decompress fix changed every file's byte
length). GET /api/media/:id serves responses with an "immutable" cache
header — a promise that the bytes at a given id never change. Reusing the
id on a real content change breaks that promise: any client that already
cached the old response has no reason to ever re-fetch, which is exactly
what made the previous fix look broken until the browser cache was
cleared by hand.

Now the id is only reused when the byte size matches what's on record
(the self-heal/no-op-retry case); a genuine change gets a fresh id, and
the superseded object is deleted so it doesn't linger unreferenced.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: Decompress individually zstd-compressed media entries
entry.content:
Decompress individually zstd-compressed media entries

Found by pulling the actual broken asset out of production D1/R2 (via
wrangler against the real account) rather than guessing further: the D1
row and R2 object were both completely correct — right size, right
content-type — but the object's *content* was still zstd-compressed raw
bytes, served as-is under an image/webp content type. `file` identified
it as "Zstandard compressed data"; decompressing it by hand produced a
perfectly valid WebP.

Modern Anki packages compress every individual media entry with zstd,
not just the collection database (confirmed: all 4,354 media entries in
the real ~100MB sample deck are compressed) — ankiImport.js already had
the exact right helper for this (maybeDecompress, already used for the
collection database) but never applied it to media bytes, so every
extracted file has always been raw still-compressed data. This affected
audio as much as images; a byte-length match (which is all earlier
manual verification checked) can't distinguish "correct" from
"consistently still-compressed on both sides."

Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: Make per-file media processing safe to retry mid-chunk
entry.content:
Make per-file media processing safe to retry mid-chunk

Cloudflare Workflow steps retry their entire callback from the top on any
transient failure, not just the part that failed. A chunk processes ~20
files in a loop inside one step — if file 12 hits a transient D1/R2
hiccup (far more likely on real distributed Cloudflare infrastructure
than in Miniflare, which is why nothing local ever exercised this), the
retry re-runs files 1-11 too. Those had already fully succeeded,
including having their temp upload deleted as the last part of
processing — so the retry immediately found "no upload" for file 1,
which this code treated as unrecoverable and aborted the entire job on
production's first fresh, error-free-looking import of the 20-card deck.

A missing temp upload is now only treated as an error when there's also
no existing media_assets row for it — otherwise it's exactly what a
retry replaying an already-finished file looks like, and processing
returns success without redoing the (already correct) work.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: Self-heal media whose D1 row exists but R2 object doesn't
entry.content:
Self-heal media whose D1 row exists but R2 object doesn't

Re-import treated a media_assets row's recorded size_bytes as proof the
actual R2 object was there, with no way to notice otherwise. This is
exactly the state the old CPU-time-limit crash could leave behind (the D1
write completing while the R2 write for that file never fully landed) —
confirmed against production: an image imported before this session's
Workflow fix was permanently broken because every later re-import kept
treating its stale metadata as "already uploaded."

Re-import now confirms the R2 object actually exists (cached per unique
filename, so a file shared across many cards costs one HEAD, not one per
card) before skipping it; if missing, it's added back to mediaNeeded so
the next upload+process cycle repairs it in place.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: Deploy the media-import Workflow worker in CI
entry.content:
Deploy the media-import Workflow worker in CI

Its own deployable unit (workflows/anki-import) that the main Pages
project now depends on via a service binding — deployed before the
Pages step so that binding's target already exists when Pages picks up
its config.

entry.title: Poll the background media-processing job during deck import
entry.content:
Poll the background media-processing job during deck import

Media upload is now a separate step from processing (previous
commits): the browser uploads files, then hands the filename list to
.../media/process and polls .../media/jobs/:id until the Workflow
finishes, instead of getting the result inline from the old
synchronous upload response. Adds a 'processing' import status and a
running done/total count for that phase.

entry.title: Move deck media processing off the synchronous request path
entry.content:
Move deck media processing off the synchronous request path

Replaces the old POST .../media handler (removed two commits ago) with
three small endpoints: upload.js does a pure R2 put per file (no D1
calls at all, so it no longer needs a subrequest-driven file-count
cap); process.js records a media_import_jobs row and hands the file
list to the media-import Workflow via a service binding
(MEDIA_IMPORT_WORKFLOW_TRIGGER, wrangler.toml); jobs/[jobId].js is
polled for status. The actual per-file work now happens inside that
Workflow's own CPU budget instead of the request's.

Also: extends deck deletion's cascade to clean up media_import_jobs
rows, and wires the Workflow worker into the D1-integration test
project as an auxiliary worker (built from its own real wrangler.toml)
so the service binding resolves in tests the same way wrangler's local
dev registry resolves it outside them.

entry.title: Add media_import_jobs table and the standalone media-import Workflow …
entry.content:
Add media_import_jobs table and the standalone media-import Workflow worker

functions/api/decks/[deckId]/media.js processed a deck's media
synchronously inside one Pages Function invocation and crashed
production twice at real-world scale — first on Cloudflare's
subrequest cap (fixed by batching), then on the CPU-time cap
("Error 1102: Worker exceeded resource limits") even with smaller
batches, because a few thousand files' worth of R2/D1 work just
doesn't fit in one invocation's budget.

Pages Functions can't define a WorkflowEntrypoint directly, so this
adds it as its own deployable Worker (workflows/anki-import),
processing files in small chunks so each step gets a fresh CPU budget
and a crash/retry doesn't lose progress. media_import_jobs is the
durable record of a run's progress that the Pages Functions side (next
commit) triggers and polls.

Not yet wired up to anything — the Pages Functions side lands next.

entry.title: Extract per-file media processing into a shared, unit-testable module
entry.content:
Extract per-file media processing into a shared, unit-testable module

The media-processing logic that used to live inline in
functions/api/decks/[deckId]/media.js is about to move into a Workflow
(a separate Worker Pages Functions can't run directly), so it needs to
be callable from both places without duplicating the D1/R2 quirks it
already works around (instr() over LIKE, asset-id reuse on re-upload).
Pulling it out first, with its own test, keeps that migration a pure
move in the next commit rather than a move-and-rewrite.

entry.title: Fix media upload crashing on Cloudflare's subrequest limit
entry.content:
Fix media upload crashing on Cloudflare's subrequest limit

Batches were sized only by total byte count (research.md §3), which let a
batch contain hundreds of small files — real Anki decks are mostly small
audio clips, so a 20MB batch could hold 700+ of them. Each file processed
by [deckId]/media.js costs several D1/R2 subrequests inside the same
Worker invocation, and Cloudflare caps that at 50 per invocation on the
Free plan (10,000 on Paid) — a large batch blew straight through it,
surfacing only as an opaque "Worker threw exception" page in production
(Miniflare, used for all local/CI testing, doesn't enforce this limit, so
nothing caught it before deploy).

Batches are now also capped by file count, conservatively low enough to
stay safe even on the Free plan regardless of which plan this is actually
deployed on.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: Fix three bugs found by a full round-trip against a real 1,501-card deck
entry.content:
Fix three bugs found by a full round-trip against a real 1,501-card deck

- media.js: D1 rejects long/complex LIKE patterns ("LIKE or GLOB pattern
  too complex") — real Anki media filenames are often long content-hash
  strings. Switched the media-reference-rewrite lookup from LIKE '%...%'
  to instr(), a plain substring check with no such limit.
- [deckId]/index.js: deleting a deck's review history via
  card_review_state WHERE card_id IN (?, ?, ...) hit D1's ~100-bound-
  parameter cap for any deck with more cards than that. Switched to a
  subquery against cards (run before cards itself is deleted in the same
  batch). Also chunks the R2 bulk-delete call, since a deck's media count
  isn't bounded either.
- import.js: re-importing a deck upserts front/back from the client's
  freshly re-parsed HTML, which still references raw filenames — this was
  silently reverting any URL rewrite a previous import's media upload had
  already applied, breaking playback for anything that hadn't changed.
  Re-import now reapplies known rewrites itself before storing.

None of these showed up against small synthetic fixtures — found by
running the actual parser and API against the real ~100MB, 1,501-card
sample deck end-to-end.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: Fix sql.js import in the real browser dev server
entry.content:
Fix sql.js import in the real browser dev server

Excluding sql.js from Vite's dependency pre-bundling (added to work around
a Vitest-only wasm-loading quirk) also disabled the CJS-to-ESM interop that
pre-bundling normally provides. sql.js's browser build
(sql-wasm-browser.js) is CommonJS-shaped with no native ESM export, so real
browser dev broke with "does not provide an export named 'default'". The
actual wasm-loading fix (instantiateWasm in ankiImport.js) doesn't depend
on this exclusion, so it's just removed.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: Add Anki deck import
entry.content:
Add Anki deck import

Lets the owner upload an Anki .apkg export and study it with the same
spaced-repetition review flow as the built-in decks. The file is parsed
entirely client-side (JSZip + fzstd + sql.js) — handling both the legacy
plain-SQLite package format and the newer Zstandard-compressed one — then
uploaded in chunks to new D1-backed deck/card/media-asset tables and an R2
bucket, staying under Cloudflare's per-request body cap. Imported card ids
are recognized by the existing review endpoints without changing the
scheduler or its schema.

Also wires the new R2 bucket's creation into the deploy workflow
(idempotent, alongside the existing D1 migration step) so no manual
Cloudflare setup is needed before this ships.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: Remove Dependabot config
entry.content:
Remove Dependabot config

Dependencies are all exact-pinned already, so there's nothing for
version-bump PRs to do — they were just noise, and each one triggers a
full deploy.yml run (pull_request has no branch filter), which is what
looked like a false deploy failure earlier.

entry.title: Lower production WaniKani sync threshold to Guru II
entry.content:
Lower production WaniKani sync threshold to Guru II

Master (srs_stage 7) was too high a bar — few words have reached it yet,
so the sync returned zero results. Guru II (6) matches local dev's default
and gives the quiz something to work with while more words mature.

entry.title: Add WaniKani-sourced listening quiz
entry.content:
Add WaniKani-sourced listening quiz

New pillar (#/listening-quiz): hear a native pronunciation recording of a
word studied on WaniKani and type its English meaning. The word cache
(meanings, readings, audio URLs) lives in D1, refreshed on demand via an
in-app "Sync from WaniKani" button calling a new Pages Function
(POST /api/wanikani-words/sync) that runs the WaniKani fetch server-side —
nothing WaniKani-sourced, including the API key, ever touches the repo.

Production's WANIKANI_API_KEY is provisioned on every deploy from a GitHub
Actions secret, validated and applied against a new
.github/prod.template.yaml manifest (deploy.yml fails fast if it's
missing). Local dev gets its own sync script (npm run sync:wanikani)
against local D1, and browser-side Cache Storage avoids re-fetching audio
already played once.

entry.title: Add Counting People (人) table to Kanji reference
entry.content:
Add Counting People (人) table to Kanji reference

Third counter table alongside days-of-the-month and things (つ). Unlike
those two, 人 mostly runs on ordinary Sino-Japanese numbers + にん, with
its irregular zone at the start (ひとり/ふたり are fully native words)
rather than the edges, plus a couple of one-off quirks (よにん drops
よん's ん; 七人 has two accepted readings).

entry.content:
